subject: Science
title: Plant Systems
learningOutcomes: Differentiate between the macro-structures of the root and shoot systems.
Explain how xylem and phloem work as the plant's transport tissues.
Explain how osmosis and root hairs help a plant absorb water from the soil.
Describe transpiration, the transpiration stream, and the factors that affect the rate of transpiration.
Explain photosynthesis and leaf structure, why plants need minerals, and the different fates of glucose.
Compare respiration with gas exchange in plants.

sections.heading: Root and Shoot Systems
sections.body: A plant's body is divided into two systems. The root system is the underground part: it anchors the plant firmly in the soil, absorbs water and minerals, and in some plants stores food. A taproot (like a carrot) is one long, thick main root growing straight down, while a fibrous root system (like grass) has many thin roots of similar size spreading out from the base. The shoot system is everything above the ground — stems, leaves, flowers, and buds. The stem supports the plant and holds the leaves up to the light, leaves make food, flowers carry out reproduction, and buds are the growing points where new growth begins.

sections.heading: Transport in Plants: Xylem and Phloem
sections.body: Plants have a transport system of thin tubes running through the roots and stems, called vascular tissues. There are two kinds. Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals in one direction only — upward from the roots to the rest of the plant. Xylem is made of dead cells with thick, strong walls, so it is essentially wood and also helps support the plant. Phloem carries dissolved sugar (food) made in the leaves to every other part of the plant, and it can move in both directions. Phloem is made of living cells joined end to end with holes at their ends. Together, xylem and phloem are grouped into vascular bundles.

sections.heading: Osmosis and Root Hairs
sections.body: Water enters a plant through its roots by osmosis — the movement of water molecules from a region of high water concentration (the soil) to a region of lower water concentration (inside the root) across a partially permeable membrane. A partially permeable membrane lets water pass but holds back other substances. Root hairs are tiny extensions of the outer root cells; they hugely increase the surface area of the roots so the plant can take in far more water and minerals from the soil.

sections.heading: Transpiration
sections.body: Transpiration is the loss of water as water vapour from the leaves of a plant. Water evaporates from cells inside the leaf and the vapour escapes through tiny holes called stomata, found mainly on the lower surface of the leaf. Each stoma is surrounded by two sausage-shaped guard cells that control its size: when the plant has plenty of water the guard cells swell and the stoma opens, and when they lose water the stoma closes. The rate of transpiration is increased by higher temperature, more wind, lower humidity, and daylight (when stomata are open).

sections.heading: The Transpiration Stream
sections.body: The transpiration stream is the continuous flow of water in the xylem from the roots up to the leaves. As water evaporates from the leaves, more water is pulled up the xylem to replace it — just like drinking through a straw. Step by step: water enters the root hairs, moves cell to cell by osmosis to the xylem, is carried up the xylem, and is finally lost from the leaves as vapour through the stomata. This stream keeps water and minerals moving throughout even a very large plant.

sections.heading: Photosynthesis and Leaf Structure
sections.body: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants make their own food. It happens in the leaves during daylight, inside tiny structures called chloroplasts that contain the green pigment chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy. Leaves are well-suited to this job: they are broad and flat to catch light, thin so gases reach every cell, full of stomata for gas exchange, and packed with veins (vascular bundles) to bring water and carry sugar away. A waxy cuticle on the transparent upper skin lets light through while preventing water loss.

sections.heading: The Process of Photosynthesis
sections.body: The raw materials for photosynthesis are carbon dioxide (which enters the leaf through stomata by diffusion) and water (carried up from the roots in the xylem). Using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll, the plant converts these into glucose and oxygen. Word equation: Carbon dioxide + Water → (light, chlorophyll) → Glucose + Oxygen. The oxygen diffuses out through the stomata into the air, and it is this oxygen that makes life on Earth possible.

sections.heading: Plants Need Minerals
sections.body: Besides carbon dioxide and water, plants need minerals from the soil for healthy growth. They use minerals to build molecules such as proteins from the glucose made in photosynthesis. For example, plants need magnesium to make chlorophyll and nitrates to make protein. Minerals in the soil come from weathered rock, from the decay of dead plants and animals and their waste, and from artificial fertilizers added by farmers to replace minerals removed by crops or washed away by rain (leaching).

sections.heading: What Happens to Glucose
sections.body: Glucose is a sugar and is the food a plant makes in photosynthesis. A plant uses its glucose in five main ways: it is broken down in respiration to release energy; it is changed into cellulose to build strong cell walls; it is stored as starch or oil in roots, stems, seeds, and fruits; it is combined with nitrogen (from nitrates) to make protein; and it is combined with magnesium to make chlorophyll. Stored starch can be changed back into sugar whenever the plant needs it.

sections.heading: Respiration in Plants
sections.body: Respiration is the release of energy from the breakdown of glucose in living cells, and it happens in every plant cell all the time, even at night. In aerobic respiration ('with air') glucose reacts with oxygen to release a lot of energy, producing carbon dioxide and water: Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy. In anaerobic respiration ('without air'), when roots are in waterlogged soil, glucose is only partly broken down into ethanol and carbon dioxide, releasing much less energy. Ethanol is toxic, so the plant must return to aerobic respiration before it builds up.

sections.heading: Gas Exchange in Plants
sections.body: Gases move in and out of a leaf through the stomata by diffusion — the movement of particles from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated. Gas exchange is complicated during the day because plants photosynthesise and respire at the same time: photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen, while respiration does the opposite. The two processes are exact opposites and complement each other, keeping the levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the air balanced. A plant needs both: photosynthesis to make food, and respiration to release the energy stored in it.

definitions.definition: The underground part of a plant that anchors it, absorbs water and minerals, and can store food.
One long, thick main root that grows straight down, as in a carrot.
Many thin roots of similar size spreading from the base of the plant, with no single main root.
All the parts of a plant above the ground: stems, leaves, flowers, and buds.
Dead, thick-walled vascular tissue that carries water and minerals upward from the roots.
Living vascular tissue that carries dissolved sugar from the leaves to all parts of the plant, in both directions.
A group of xylem and phloem tubes bundled together inside stems and roots.
The movement of water molecules from a region of high water concentration to a lower one across a partially permeable membrane.
Tiny extensions of the outer root cells that increase surface area for absorbing water and minerals.
A thin layer that lets some substances (like water) pass through but not others.
The loss of water as water vapour from the leaves of a plant, mainly through the stomata.
Tiny holes, mainly on the lower side of a leaf, that let gases and water vapour pass in and out.
A pair of cells around each stoma that open and close it by gaining or losing water.
The continuous flow of water in the xylem from the roots to the leaves.
The green pigment in leaves that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
A tiny structure in leaf cells, containing chlorophyll, where photosynthesis takes place.
A waxy layer on the upper skin of a leaf that makes it waterproof.
The process by which plants use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
The use of energy to move minerals into root cells against the concentration gradient.
The washing of dissolved minerals downward through the soil and out of reach of roots.
The release of energy from the breakdown of glucose in living cells.
The movement of particles from a region of high concentration to one of low concentration.

interactiveLesson.instructions: Explore each labelled part of the plant. Select every hotspot to continue.

hotspots.label: Root Hairs
hotspots.fact: Root hairs are tiny extensions of the root's outer cells. They greatly increase surface area so the plant can absorb more water and minerals from the soil.

hotspots.label: Root System
hotspots.fact: The root system anchors the plant, absorbs water and minerals, and stores food in some plants.

hotspots.label: Xylem
hotspots.fact: Xylem is made of dead, thick-walled cells and carries water and minerals upward from the roots. It also helps support the plant.

hotspots.label: Phloem
hotspots.fact: Phloem is made of living cells and carries dissolved sugar from the leaves to the rest of the plant, in both directions.

hotspots.label: Stem
hotspots.fact: The stem supports the plant above ground and holds the leaves up to the light and the flowers up to attract insects.

hotspots.label: Leaf
hotspots.fact: Leaves are broad, flat and thin — ideal for absorbing light and exchanging gases. They are the main site of photosynthesis.

hotspots.label: Stomata & Guard Cells
hotspots.fact: Stomata are tiny holes, mostly on the lower leaf surface. Two guard cells open and close each stoma to control gas exchange and transpiration.

hotspots.label: Flower
hotspots.fact: Flowers contain the reproductive organs. Bright petals and scent attract insects for pollination.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which of these is part of the shoot system?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The shoot system is everything above ground: stems, leaves, flowers, and buds.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which tissue carries water and minerals upward and is made of dead cells?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Xylem is made of dead, thick-walled cells and carries water and minerals upward only.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Phloem carries sugar and can move it in both directions.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Phloem is living tissue and transports sugar both up and down the plant.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Water enters the root by ____, moving from high to low water concentration.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Osmosis moves water across the partially permeable root membrane into the root.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why do roots have root hairs?

options: To increase surface area for absorption

practiceQuestions.explanation: Root hairs increase surface area so more water and minerals can be absorbed.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Through which structures is most water lost during transpiration?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Water vapour escapes mainly through the stomata on the lower leaf surface.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Transpiration speeds up on humid days.
practiceQuestions.explanation: High humidity slows transpiration; dry air speeds it up.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Match each part to its job:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Each structure has a specific transport or exchange role.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What are the two products of photosynthesis?
The green pigment that absorbs light for photosynthesis is ____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Chlorophyll in the chloroplasts absorbs light energy.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which mineral do plants need to make chlorophyll?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Magnesium is combined with glucose to make chlorophyll.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Glucose combined with nitrogen from nitrates is used to make:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Nitrogen from nitrates joins glucose to make protein.
Respiration happens in every living cell all the time, day and night.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Anaerobic respiration in plant cells produces:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Without oxygen, glucose breaks down only to ethanol and carbon dioxide, releasing less energy.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Arrange the journey of water from soil to air:

items: Water is carried up the xylem
Water moves cell to cell to the xylem
Water vapour leaves through the stomata
correctOrder: Water moves cell to cell to the xylem
Water is carried up the xylem
Water vapour leaves through the stomata

practiceQuestions.explanation: This is the transpiration stream from soil to leaf to air.

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange the stages of the transpiration stream in order, from soil to air.

items: Water is pulled up the xylem
Water enters the root hairs by osmosis
Water vapour escapes through the stomata
Water moves cell to cell toward the xylem
Water evaporates from leaf cells into air spaces
correctOrder: Water enters the root hairs by osmosis
Water moves cell to cell toward the xylem
Water is pulled up the xylem
Water evaporates from leaf cells into air spaces
Water vapour escapes through the stomata

sequencingActivity.explanation: Water travels soil → root hairs → xylem → leaf → out through stomata as vapour.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Xylem is made of dead cells with thick walls. Which statement best explains why this suits its job?

options: Hollow, strong tubes let water flow freely and support the plant

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Empty dead cells form clear tubes for water, and thick walls give strength and support.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A plant is moved from a cool, still, humid room to a warm, windy, dry balcony. What happens to its transpiration rate?
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Higher temperature, wind, and low humidity all speed up transpiration.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Why can't a plant absorb most minerals by osmosis alone?

options: There are usually more minerals inside the root than in the soil, so energy is needed to pull them in

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Minerals are often more concentrated inside root cells, so active transport (using energy) moves them against the gradient.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Why are the photosynthesis and respiration equations described as exact opposites?

options: The products of one are the reactants of the other
They both happen only at night

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Photosynthesis makes glucose and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water; respiration reverses this, keeping the air balanced.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A plant's roots are in waterlogged soil for a long time. Why is this dangerous?

options: Too much oxygen reaches the roots
Anaerobic respiration builds up toxic ethanol that can kill the plant

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Without oxygen the plant respires anaerobically, and the ethanol produced is toxic if it builds up.
